L_alarm.title: Alarm features — evaluate before treating empirically
L_alarm.rec: Dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, GI bleeding, or anemia alongside acid symptoms warrant endoscopic evaluation before starting or escalating empiric acid suppression.
L_alarm.why: These features raise the likelihood of a structural or malignant cause that acid suppression alone would mask rather than address.

L_mild_gerd.title: Mild, infrequent GERD
L_mild_gerd.rec: Lifestyle measures (weight, meal timing, trigger avoidance) plus as-needed antacids or an H2 blocker are often sufficient before reaching for a PPI.
L_mild_gerd.why: Reserving PPIs for more frequent or severe symptoms avoids unnecessary long-term acid suppression for a problem that may not need it.

L_gerd_standard.title: Standard once-daily PPI trial
L_gerd_standard.rec: A standard-dose PPI taken 30–60 minutes before the first meal, for a defined trial period (commonly 4–8 weeks), is the typical starting point.
L_gerd_standard.why: Pre-meal dosing maximizes the number of actively secreting pumps available for irreversible binding.

L_gerd_clopidogrel.title: PPI choice matters here
L_gerd_clopidogrel.rec: Pantoprazole is generally preferred over omeprazole/esomeprazole given its lower CYP2C19 interaction potential.
L_gerd_clopidogrel.why: Reduces the theoretical risk of blunting clopidogrel’s antiplatelet activation.

L_gerd_dexlansoprazole.title: Flexible-timing option
L_gerd_dexlansoprazole.rec: Dexlansoprazole’s dual delayed-release formulation allows dosing without strict regard to meals.
L_gerd_dexlansoprazole.why: The two-pulse release profile removes the pre-meal timing requirement that limits other PPIs.

L_refractory.title: Refractory GERD despite standard PPI
L_refractory.rec: First confirm adherence and timing are correct; if truly refractory, a PCAB or specialist referral for pH/impedance testing is reasonable.
L_refractory.why: PCABs achieve more complete, more consistent acid suppression — including overnight — without needing acid-catalyzed activation.

L_nsaid_ulcer.title: NSAID-associated ulcer
L_nsaid_ulcer.rec: Stop the NSAID if possible and treat with a PPI course; if the NSAID must continue, co-prescribe a PPI long-term or consider a COX-2 selective agent if cardiovascular risk is low.
L_nsaid_ulcer.why: Removing the causative agent, where feasible, matters as much as acid suppression itself.

L_hpylori.title: H. pylori eradication
L_hpylori.rec: A combination regimen — a PPI or PCAB plus multiple antibiotics — for roughly 10–14 days, with the specific combination guided by local resistance patterns.
L_hpylori.why: Acid suppression alone doesn’t eradicate H. pylori; it’s combined with antibiotics both to improve antibiotic stability in the stomach and to support mucosal healing.
L_hpylori.caution: This reference doesn’t specify an exact regimen — eradication protocols vary by local resistance and current guidelines.

L_ulcer_general.title: Ulcer, cause unclear
L_ulcer_general.rec: Test for H. pylori and review medication history (including over-the-counter NSAID or aspirin use) before starting empiric acid suppression.
L_ulcer_general.why: Identifying the cause changes the whole management plan, not just the acid-suppression choice.

L_nsaid_low_risk.title: Low GI-risk NSAID use
L_nsaid_low_risk.rec: Gastroprotection is often unnecessary for short, low-risk courses — use the lowest effective NSAID dose for the shortest reasonable duration.
L_nsaid_low_risk.why: Routine co-prescribing for every NSAID course isn’t evidence-based when baseline risk is low.

L_nsaid_high_risk.title: High GI-risk NSAID use
L_nsaid_high_risk.rec: Co-prescribe a PPI for the duration of NSAID therapy, or consider a COX-2 selective agent if cardiovascular risk is also low.
L_nsaid_high_risk.why: Risk factors compound — age, prior ulcer, and concurrent anticoagulant/steroid use each independently raise GI bleeding risk.

q_start.q: What’s the predominant lesion type and severity?

Mostly post-inflammatory marks, few active lesions
Tried a retinoid alone without enough benefit after 8–12 weeks

A_comedonal.title: Comedonal acne
A_comedonal.rec: A topical retinoid as monotherapy — adapalene is a reasonable, well-tolerated starting point — introduced gradually to manage the initial purge.
A_comedonal.why: Comedonal acne is primarily a keratinization problem; a retinoid addresses that mechanism directly without needing an antimicrobial partner yet.

A_mild_first_line.title: Mild-moderate inflammatory acne — first line
A_mild_first_line.rec: A fixed-combination topical — typically a retinoid plus benzoyl peroxide — as the starting regimen.
A_mild_first_line.why: Combining a comedolytic and an antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory agent targets two separate pathogenic steps at once, which is why combinations outperform either ingredient alone.

A_mild_escalate.title: Escalating beyond a retinoid alone
A_mild_escalate.rec: Add benzoyl peroxide, or a topical antibiotic always paired with benzoyl peroxide, to the existing retinoid rather than switching retinoids first.
A_mild_escalate.why: Most "retinoid failure" at this stage is a missing second mechanism, not the wrong retinoid choice.

A_moderate_standard.title: Moderate-severe inflammatory acne
A_moderate_standard.rec: Topical retinoid + benzoyl peroxide as the ongoing backbone, plus a capped course (commonly a few months) of an oral antibiotic as a bridge, with a plan to step back down to topical maintenance once controlled.
A_moderate_standard.why: Oral antibiotics are meant to be time-limited — see the maintenance vs. flare framework.

A_pregnancy_safe.title: Pregnancy-safe regimen
A_pregnancy_safe.rec: Azelaic acid as a core agent, given its established pregnancy safety profile; avoid oral and topical retinoids, oral tetracyclines, and isotretinoin entirely.
A_pregnancy_safe.why: Retinoids (all forms) and tetracyclines both carry pregnancy contraindications discussed in their individual entries.

A_moderate_pigmentation.title: Active acne with concurrent pigmentation
A_moderate_pigmentation.rec: Azelaic acid or a retinoid alongside standard inflammatory acne therapy — both offer a genuine PIH benefit — rather than treating pigmentation only after acne clears.
A_moderate_pigmentation.why: Turnover-based and tyrosinase-based pigment mechanisms can run in parallel with standard inflammatory treatment rather than waiting for it to finish.

A_severe.title: Severe / scarring-risk acne
A_severe.rec: Refer for consideration of isotretinoin — the only option here aiming for durable remission rather than ongoing management — particularly given scarring risk. Topical and oral bridge therapy are reasonable while awaiting evaluation, not substitutes for it.
A_severe.why: Scarring risk changes the urgency calculus: delay itself carries a cost that milder acne doesn’t.

A_marks.title: Mostly post-inflammatory marks
A_marks.rec: Redirect toward pigment-modulating agents (azelaic acid, niacinamide, or hydroquinone for stubborn marks) and daily sunscreen, rather than escalating antibacterial or anti-inflammatory therapy the current picture doesn’t need.
A_marks.why: Marks and active lesions need different tools — treating a resolved mark like active acne wastes the antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory strategy on a problem it can’t solve.
